title: This Is Something You Need To Know About Yourself
author: Ryan Holiday
summary: Ryan Holiday opens with a story of failing to say no after a tiring talk, when an event's organizers kept adding photos, a testimonial and a client lunch until he had been fleeced of his time. Despite years of writing about the discipline of saying no, he found he could not do it that day because he was tired, alone and surrounded by friendly people. Drawing on Angela Duckworth's book Situated, he argues that behavior is situational and that we are not the same person in every setting. The remedy he draws from the ancient command to know thyself is to learn when you decide well and when you do not, and then arrange your environment around that knowledge. He supports this with Arthur MacArthur's telegram about a bribe and Toni Morrison's question about the ideal conditions for creative work. His closing instruction is to know the people and places that bring out your best, and your worst.
points: Holiday's failure to say no shows that even a practiced discipline collapses when fatigue, isolation and friendly pressure combine.
Following Angela Duckworth, he holds that behavior is situational, so willpower and grit alone are not enough without the right conditions.
Knowing yourself means identifying when you decide well, when you need a buffer or a helper, and when to leave a situation.
Captain Arthur MacArthur's telegram asking for relief because they were getting close to his price models acting on self-knowledge before a bribe works.
Noticing your worst times, such as afternoons for writing or skipped weekend workouts, lets you protect what matters by design.
quotes: None of it was a huge imposition by itself, but it’s not stuff I normally agree to. I’m usually pretty good about saying “No” to things I don’t want to do—especially points that are usually, in the speaking world, points of a contract—but I was exhausted and I was alone and they were friendly.
Yes, grit is important. Yes, discipline is a skill. Yes, we have to be able to do hard things. But we must also understand: behavior is situational. We’re not the same person in every situation.

Someone who is patient at work might be short-tempered at home. Someone who is outgoing around one group of people might be introverted around another. Someone who can say no easily in some settings might struggle to say it in others.
Knowing when you make good decisions and when you don’t is key. When you can trust yourself and when you can’t. When you need a buffer or a helper, and when you do better on your own.
I request immediate relief from this command,” he told his superiors. “They are getting close to my price.

Noticing that I almost never get good writing done in the afternoons has been helpful too. Noticing that if I don’t work out in the mornings on the weekends, I tend not to be able to find the time to do it at all (or when I do, it’s a miserable slog) has meant that I fiercely protect that time.
You gotta know your weaknesses and make decisions so you can be strong. You gotta know what brings out your worst and arrange things so you can be at your best.
